title: N2 · Unit 8

lessons.title: Follow a story through short responses
lessons.description: Hear an ordinary café plan with acknowledgements, hesitation and brief overlaps.
lessons.canDo: Separate a reaction from a reason or a settled plan

grammar.title: A short response can keep the story going
grammar.formation: へえ reacts to new information; そうなんだ acknowledges it; なるほど often marks newly understood grounds. Follow the next clause before inferring agreement.
grammar.explanation: These short turns show the listener is following, surprised or making sense of a reason. They do not by themselves promise to do an action. The same expression can be flat, interested or sceptical depending on delivery. In these scenes, a short response sometimes begins just before the other voice finishes. Listen through it for the fact or decision that follows. This is applied listening practice with earlier forms, not a newly official N2 grammar list.
grammar.example: へえ、そんなに早く開くんだ。

examples.ja: へえ、そんなに{早|はや}く{開|あ}くんだ。
そうなんだ。じゃあ、{木曜|もくよう}にしよう。
examples.en: I see. Then let’s make it Thursday.

examples.ja: なるほど、{窓|まど}を{閉|し}めたから{静|しず}かなんだね。
examples.en: That explains it: it’s quiet because you shut the window.

grammar.mistake: A short acknowledgement does not answer every question with yes. Hear the following clause, and do not insert the same reaction after every sentence.

grammar.title: Hear the thought after a hesitation
grammar.formation: えっと / あの + a searched-for word or phrase. Sentence-opening なんか can frame a tentative impression; まあ can soften a provisional judgement.
grammar.explanation: A person looking for a time, a description or a decision may hesitate. Listen for the content after the filler rather than treating the hesitation as a new topic. なんか can also be 何か meaning something, or follow a noun in a dismissive or listing expression. Its place and the whole clause decide the reading. Fillers have several uses; these scenes give particular examples, not fixed one-word translations or a rule that all hesitation is uncertainty about truth.
grammar.example: えっと、木曜の二時なら空いてる。
grammar.translation: Um, I’m free Thursday at two.

examples.ja: えっと、{木曜|もくよう}の{二時|にじ}なら{空|あ}いてる。
examples.en: Um, I’m free Thursday at two.

examples.ja: なんか、{前|まえ}より{明|あか}るくなったね。
examples.en: It somehow feels brighter than before.

examples.ja: まあ、{二人|ふたり}なら{座|すわ}れると{思|おも}う。
examples.en: Well, I think the two of us can get seats.

grammar.mistake: Do not translate every なんか as something or every まあ as agreement. A tentative impression is not a confirmed reservation.

grammar.title: Recover the missing noun from this conversation
grammar.formation: A known noun may be left out after possessive の; adjective + の names the one with that property. A short predicate may omit a contextually clear person or object.
grammar.explanation: In a conversation about umbrellas, 青いの means the blue umbrella, while 美咲の can mean Misaki’s umbrella. Neither の tells you what the object is without context. If several objects or owners fit, ask which one. Omitting a recoverable noun is different from removing every case particle: casual speech can omit some particles, but not arbitrary parts of a place or role. In formal writing, make important roles clear. Earlier N5 の is retrieved at natural pace.

examples.ja: その{傘|かさ}、{美咲|みさき}の？
もう{送|おく}った？ うん、{今朝|けさ}。
examples.en: Have you sent it? Yes, this morning.

grammar.mistake: Do not assume an omitted actor is always the last named person. Resolve the current question and situation, or request clarification.

grammar.title: Check a reference and repair the misunderstanding
grammar.formation: どの…？ / …って、…？ / もう一度…？ asks about an unclear item or turn. Acknowledgement can be followed by a correction or refusal.
grammar.explanation: Friends often use a short clarification rather than repeat the whole previous sentence. Name the unclear item when asking. When Kenta says he can return the umbrella this evening, そうなんだ acknowledges that information; でも、今日は無理 then rejects the proposed time. Understanding and agreement are separate. These are context-based reply skills using known question and negative forms, not a rule to infer a refusal from every unfinished sentence.
grammar.translation: By the blue one, do you mean the umbrella by the entrance?

examples.ja: {青|あお}いのって、{入口|いりぐち}の{傘|かさ}？
examples.en: By the blue one, do you mean the umbrella by the entrance?

examples.ja: そうなんだ。でも、{今日|きょう}は{無理|むり}。{明日|あした}ならいいよ。
examples.en: I see. But today won’t work. Tomorrow is fine.

examples.ja: {何時|なんじ}って{言|い}った？ {聞|き}こえなかった。
examples.en: What time did you say? I couldn’t hear it.

grammar.mistake: Acknowledging someone’s information is not permission for their proposal. Hear the following clause. When the reference stays unclear, ask rather than guessing an owner or plan.

dialogues.title: A café, a postcard and a Thursday plan

recycling.reason: These friends discuss a café and two umbrellas after three formal news/office units. 宛先 is genuinely retrieved in the postcard reading; forcing their unrelated committee or procurement vocabulary into casual turns would make the scene artificial. Older café, colour, time and loan vocabulary is reused extensively. The recent-three-unit target is deliberately reduced to three percent; supplementary conversation vocabulary stays outside the scene quota.

watch.prompt: Optionally listen to your own familiar scene. Follow one exchange without the transcript, then check which short replies merely acknowledge and which settle an action. Replay a short overlap instead of guessing a missing word.
